posts.author: Diogo António
posts.snippet:
O caso Hezbollah/Tajideen deixa uma mensagem importante:

Uma operação pode parecer comercialmente legítima e, ainda assim, representar um risco significativo de Financiamento ao Terrorismo.

Por isso, KYC não pode ser apenas “conhecer o cliente”.
É necessário compreender:
👉 Quem controla realmente a empresa?
👉 Qual é a origem dos fundos?
👉 Qual é a finalidade económica da operação?
👉 Para onde o dinheiro está a ser enviado?
👉 Quem é o beneficiário final?
👉 Existem ligações com pessoas ou entidades sancionadas?
👉 O comportamento transaccional é compatível com o perfil do cliente?

Para os profissionais de Compliance, AML/CFT, Risco e Auditoria, a prevenção começa muito antes de uma operação ser considerada suspeita.
Começa com conhecimento do cliente, identificação do beneficiário efectivo, avaliação baseada no risco, monitorização contínua e uma cultura de Compliance verdadeiramente eficaz.
🇦🇴 Para Angola, esta discussão é particularmente relevante.
O combate ao Financiamento do Terrorismo não é apenas uma obrigação regulatória. É também uma questão de segurança nacional, integridade do sistema financeiro, reputação internacional e confiança dos investidores.
Compliance não é apenas cumprir regras.
É impedir que o sistema financeiro seja utilizado para fins que podem colocar pessoas, instituições e sociedades em risco.

posts.title: Bailey es una beagle genéticamente modificada desarrollada por Kindred Companion Sciences.
posts.author: Nicolás Villarroel Jorquera
posts.snippet:
Bailey es una beagle genéticamente modificada desarrollada por Kindred Companion Sciences.

Nació en septiembre de 2024 junto a su gemelo Alfie. Ambos fueron creados mediante CRISPR-Cas9 para eliminar el gen responsable de producir Can f 1, uno de los principales alérgenos del perro, identificado y denominado como tal en 1991.

Las pruebas no detectaron Can f 1 en saliva, pelo ni caspa. Además, una prueba cutánea realizada en una persona alérgica no mostró reacción.

En gatos ocurre algo similar: existen múltiples alérgenos, pero Fel d 1 es el principal y ya era reconocido clínicamente en la década de 1980.

CRISPR-Cas9, tecnología detrás de este avance, recibió el Nobel de Química en 2020.

No significa que Bailey sea completamente “hipoalergénica”. Significa que, por primera vez, se está intentando abordar la alergia al perro desde su origen genético.

posts.title: Many boards have taken the cautious position on AI. Watch and observe, but resist adoption and tool provision within the business, avoiding the risk of being blamed when AI gets it
posts.author: David Royle
posts.snippet:
Many boards have taken the cautious position on AI. Watch and observe, but resist adoption and tool provision within the business, avoiding the risk of being blamed when AI gets it wrong. It plays to the stories that fill the press: AI misused, undue reliance placed on it, mistakes made. 

A legal statement published earlier this year says the opposite. Doing nothing could now be negligent.

We came across it while researching how AI is being used and regulated across the legal sector. What struck us wasn't just the finding, though that's significant enough on its own. It was how little coverage it's had. Search business press, search LinkedIn, search the usual governance commentary, and this barely features. So I'm sharing it directly.

It comes from the UK Jurisdiction Taskforce, under the chairmanship of Sir Geoffrey Vos, Master of the Rolls and Head of Civil Justice for England and Wales. This isn't a think tank paper or a vendor whitepaper. The UKJT produced the 2019 Legal Statement on Cryptoassets and Smart Contracts, the document English courts leaned on to shape how crypto was treated years before Parliament touched the subject. This is the same exercise, aimed at AI, drafted by a panel of King's Counsel and legal academics, publicly consulted before release.

The headline conclusion is reassuring. England and Wales doesn't need new AI-specific law. Existing principles of negligence, contract and professional liability already cover harm caused by AI.

What follows from that is less comfortable, and it isn't limited to regulated doctors, lawyers and accountants.

Anyone who owes a duty of reasonable skill and care could now have that duty measured against AI use. Careless use could be negligence. So, on the Statement's own reasoning, could failing to use AI where a reasonably competent peer would have. Its example: a radiologist who doesn't use an AI system proven highly effective at spotting tumours, despite it being available at reasonable cost. Nothing reckless there. Just standing still while the profession moved on.

It goes wider than professional advice. The Statement is explicit that an employer could be held vicariously liable when an employee causes harm while using AI, in exactly the same way an employer answers for any other action its staff take at work. That reaches every business with people using AI tools, not just the regulated professions with an obvious duty of care.

None of this has been tested in court yet. But it's the clearest signal so far of how a court is likely to reason when it is, from the same body whose last major statement proved a reliable guide to where the law went next.

Restriction is starting to look like the riskier position, not the safer one.
Is your caution protecting the business, or exposing it?
posts.reason: UK legal statement on AI liability and negligence is directly relevant to deep tech and AI Act readiness, and targets GCs and compliance leads considering AI implementation risk.

comments.text: We saw the same pattern with the 2019 UKJT Statement on crypto: courts and boards ignored it until it quietly became the reference point in disputes. The AI Statement's negligence angle is the sharper read, because it shifts the risk calculus from 'did we misuse AI' to 'did we fail to use a tool a competent peer would have used'.

Do you think boards will actually treat 'failure to adopt' as a live negligence exposure before a court tests it, or will this sit unused the way plenty of soft-law statements do until the first claim forces the point?

We get the same silence when we flag MiCAR's white paper duties to clients who assume 'no enforcement yet' means 'no exposure yet' — the gap between publication and market attention on these statements is often a year or more.

Shared devices, contact details, intermediaries and counterparties may reveal relationships that conventional customer-level monitoring does not identify. posts.title: Justice in the courtroom can instantly be paralyzed in the face of mathematical sovereignty.
posts.author: Muhammad Fakhri Amal
posts.snippet:
Justice in the courtroom can instantly be paralyzed in the face of mathematical sovereignty.

Last Friday, I had the honor of presenting my academic paper titled The Jurisdictional Limits of Islamic Inheritance Law: Facing the Absolutism of Private Keys in the Execution of Crypto Asset Disputes in the Digital Era ( Batas Yurisdiksi Hukum Waris Islam: Menghadapi Absolutisme Kunci Privat dalam Eksekusi Sengketa Aset Kripto di Era Digital ) at the panel session on National Seminar hosted by Faculty of Islamic Religious Studies (FIAI), Universitas Islam Indonesia (UII).

Before panelists, I highlighted an operational reality that remains a massive blind spot in our family law system: How can the Religious Court execute the distribution of inheritance (Tirkah) or marital assets if the object is a self-custody crypto portfolio worth billions of rupiah, and the deceased took their Private Key to the grave?

The truth is, the court is paralyzed. A final, legally binding ruling loses its executorial power entirely when clashing with the architecture of the blockchain. Cryptographic systems do not care about court orders or inheritance certificates.

The response from the academic forum was highly validating and served as a wake-up call. There was a clear consensus that state authority has an absolute limit in cyberspace. Educating the public about digital inheritance mitigation is no longer optional, it is a critical necessity.

As a Private Legacy Counsel, this is my core mission. We must shift the dispute resolution paradigm toward preventive measures. We need to integrate advanced security protocols like Split-Custody with Sharia-compliant inheritance laws (Hifdzul Maal), long before the lack of access turns family wealth into permanently lost assets (Maal Dha'i).
Thank you to the organizers for this incredible intellectual discourse. Let us prepare for the new era of family financial sovereignty.

The binder has been closed. I have completed the Australian Institute of Company Directors' Company Directors Course and been awarded the GAICD designation.

My warmest thanks to Sue Craig FAICD and Paola Tesolin AAICD, who first introduced me to the AICD and encouraged me to complete the course.

A word on the pre-reading and the infamous binder that I have seen many times on LinkedIn - even though it was big enough to block out the sun, it was absorbing in a way I did not expect. By the time the final week of pre-reading came, I was delighted to have a better grasp of the fundamentals of governance, and of its language - specific parts of finance and law.

I will admit, walking into a room of seasoned executives and directors was initially intimidating. That lasted until the discussion started, which turned out to be the best part of the course, and I found myself contributing rather than just observing. My thanks to my cohort and facilitators for the generosity with which they shared judgement earned over decades in the chair, and for the openness that made that possible.

Governance conversations increasingly run in both directions between Australia and APAC-connected companies. What I valued most about the course was how clearly it set out what an Australian board expects of the people who support it, and I intend to hold that standard in every room I work in.

Onwards — and, evidently, with a good deal more reading ahead.

posts.title: What would a Union of 30+ member states look like? How can the EU integrate new members? The Commission is preparing its proposal ahead of the October European leaders' meeting to
posts.author: Luca Bertuzzi
posts.snippet:
What would a Union of 30+ member states look like? How can the EU integrate new members? The Commission is preparing its proposal ahead of the October European leaders' meeting to discuss these key questions. European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos gave a preview today. 

First, internal reforms. Kos suggested that the EU decision-making process needs to be made leaner, including moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting and making the institutions leaner - stopping short of suggesting the one country, one Commissioner rule would need to be dropped.  Crucially, she said such changes could be done without changing the treaties. 

Second, stronger safeguards against democratic and rule-of-law backsliding, as suggested by the five founding members. Kos didn't provide details on how to avoid breaching the principle of equality of EU countries.  "We must make sure we do not let in Trojan horses. posts.title: She spent more than a decade working across law, finance and complex transactions before becoming COO of a digital asset infrastructure company.
posts.author: Eleonora Ferrero
posts.snippet:
She spent more than a decade working across law, finance and complex transactions before becoming COO of a digital asset infrastructure company.

Now she is rebuilding how that company operates by going after one of the less visible costs of scaling: the work required just to move information around.

Meet Lily Z. King, COO of Cobo.
Cobo operates across R&D, operations, compliance and customer service. As it grew, information scattered across those teams and had to be re-explained before decisions could be made.

Lily treated that coordination layer itself as the problem to fix.

Every employee got LLM access. Training taught people to spot information-heavy, cross-team processes worth redesigning. Staff from business, operations and support then built agents around problems they knew firsthand.

One of them looks at client service quality.

Staff used to monitor communications and rely on their own read of satisfaction. Now the agent reads context and sentiment and produces a summary the organisation can use.

For Lily, the interesting part went beyond the time saved.

Knowledge that used to sit with individual employees became a reusable organisational capability.

And then she saw something bigger: a process that once needed several teams to assemble context compressed into a single input for a decision.

"The organisational chain had suddenly shortened."

Lily is redesigning that layer of Cobo, so people spend less time preparing the organisation to decide and more time deciding and executing.

The work changes because the operating model changes first.

As information processing gets cheaper, human value shifts to knowing what should be done, deciding whether the result is good enough, and turning it into action.

Lily redesigned Cobo's coordination layer so decisions no longer had to wait on it.

That is the operating lesson.

comments.text: The shift she describes maps almost exactly onto what we see when startups scale compliance functions in crypto and deep tech: the bottleneck is rarely the analysis itself but re-explaining context to the next person in the chain.

Interesting - once agents compress that coordination layer, who ends up owning the decision when the agent's summary turns out to be wrong? That accountability question doesn't disappear with the process.

We see the same pattern in legal work: half the time on a token classification opinion goes not into the analysis but into reassembling scattered documentation and context across teams before we can even start.

If you have a little extra time to spare in your day, Professor Nita Farahany is giving everyone the chance to audit on Substack, free of charge, the same AI Law and Policy class she is delivering to her students at Duke Law School this Fall Semester.

Over the course of 13 weeks, students will be challenged to think and write about the fundamentals of AI, along with the transparency, power, safety, and privacy concerns attached to it. You don't have to have a legal, policy, or tech background. This is for all citizens of good will who wish to arm themselves with the frameworks and vocabulary to contribute to the conversation around the technologies reshaping human life as profoundly as those of the Industrial Revolution.

The first lecture asks everyone to think about what AI is, and the first homework assignment is to write a 1-paragraph legal definition of AI. After some thought, I decided that the term AI should be understood to encompass "any machine-based system that processes digital information, mapping inputs to observable outputs by means of mathematical mappings that are not reducible by a reasonably skilled mathematician to closed-form functions of individual components, but rather emerge from complex statistical interactions and dependencies among the distributed parameters, representations, or data used to configure the system."

How would you define AI?

MAGNA CARTA DIGITALIS Great Charter - Digital Version

800 years ago, Magna Carta said: power must have limits. Rights must be protected. Let your imagination soar. Andy Burnham on Parliament Green, brought to heel by a large group of MPs, and he signs solemn undertakings banning the state's expropriation of client account interest and mindless digitalisation of homebuying.

So in our ideal world, a new digital charter would contain five non-negotiable principles for policy-makers and greedy law tech barons:

1. TOTAL DATA RESPONSIBILITY
If you produce the data, you own the risk. "For guidance only" cannot survive in a digital system.

2. NO BLACK BOXES
Every automated decision must be explainable and auditable. "The algorithm said so" is not a legal defence.

3. DATA SOVEREIGNTY
Client data belongs to the client and the firm. No use for training, no lock-in, UK hosted.

4. NO DIGITAL MONOPOLIES
We must not repeat what happened in Australia, where one private platform was given exclusive access to the Land Registry. No single commercial platform should control access to the Land Registry. Competition must be protected by law.

5. HUMAN JUDGMENT
AI assists. Regulated humans decide. Human-in-the-loop represents a critical duty of care, not delay. 

The roadmap is set. Now comes the hard part, the detail. Most property lawyers are ready to work with the Government, to digitise where appropriate and with the public protected.

The Government has settled on its digital roadmap for homebuying. The question is no longer whether we digitise, but how we implement it. If we get the implementation wrong, we will digitise risk and hand 100% of it to the public. If we get it right, we modernise homebuying with accountability and integrity locked in.

Apollo Global Management's recent data breach illustrates one important lesson: the absolute necessity of always being proactive. Between July 6-10 2026, hackers accessed cloud platforms containing names, birth dates, addresses and Social Security numbers. How did this happen? The entry point was not a complex AI attack, but a series of phone calls—what is known as a "low-tech" tactic that, according to experts, is still remarkably effective.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐂𝐚𝐧 𝐖𝐞 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧❓ 

🔐 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐞 𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞. The breach was detected only after external intelligence flagged suspicious activity. Proactive monitoring across cloud environments would have alerted suspicious activity in time, and this security measure is non-negotiable.
 
🔐 𝐁𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫. While Apollo acted swiftly, the GDPR has a strict 72-hour reporting rule. Organisations must have clear protocols to assess and report breaches and be ready to do so within regulatory windows, or, failing that, face significant fines.
 
🔐𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞. Apollo retained highly sensitive personal data, such as Social Security numbers. Under the GDPR principle of Data Minimisation, organisations should always seek to minimise the amount of data collected and retained. The less data there is, the lower the risk of exposure.
 
Cybercriminals are beginning to cast a wider net, aiming to hack and target organisations such as Uber, Levi Strauss and dozens of financial firms. This growing trend of cyber-crime suggests that investing equally in employee training, incident response planning and third-party threat intelligence is crucial in order to prevent such huge data loss.

She acknowledged the dissonance. ‘We are in it for the good of the students and for the good of the country and for the good of families and to make sure educators actually play their rightful role,' she said. This reflected concerns around fiscal borrowing needs, oil prices, and sustained long-end supply.

Treasury Secretary Bessent’s plan to expand purchases of longer-dated Treasuries was aimed at easing upward pressure on yields rather than replicating traditional quantitative easing. The policy shift also highlights the growing importance of short-term borrowing costs and the shape of the yield curve in managing federal interest expense.

Markets also responded to renewed geopolitical uncertainty surrounding Iran and energy supply. Oil strengthened, with WTI and Brent finishing at $82.40 and $88.52 per barrel, respectively. Real growth is hidden inside. Not in numbers, mentions, or how many people are writing X threads about the project.

Growth is measured in retention, and retention is what drives growth.

You can get thousands of followers in a few days. That doesn't solve the growth problem on the product side.

The real questions are simple. How many people actually use the product. 

How many will still be using it next month. 
How many will advocate for it because they use it, not because they were paid to talk about it.

This is why big companies that raised big still wind down within months.

OlympusDAO is a good example. It had a massive following, a token that pumped hard, and a treasury everyone talked about. 

But the growth was built on APY, not on people who needed the product. Once the yield slowed down, retention collapsed with it.

Wonderland (TIME) is another. Huge community, huge hype, a treasury in the billions at one point. 

But there was no real usage behind the noise. When the hype faded, so did everyone in it.

So both had attention but neither had retention. That's the difference between growth that looks real and growth that is real.

If your product can't hold the people who already found it, more followers won't save it.

It's unfortunate that many web3 teams are optimising so much for vanity metrics over real growth.

posts.title: Nigeria's SEC has moved the minimum capital requirement for digital asset exchanges and custodians from N500 million to N2 billion.
posts.author: Africa Web3 Institute
posts.snippet:
Nigeria's SEC has moved the minimum capital requirement for digital asset exchanges and custodians from N500 million to N2 billion. 

Draft rules released on 20 August add a N30 million registration fee and a fidelity insurance bond covering 25% of that capital floor.

Institutionally backed exchanges have the capital to meet this. Smaller operators don't.

The OTC and peer-to-peer networks handling a large share of Nigeria's actual crypto volume don't have it either—the volume that built Nigeria's reputation as one of Africa's most active crypto economies now exceeds what this rule allows.

In 2021, central bank restrictions on crypto banking pushed volume into P2P channels rather than shutting it down. 

A capital requirement four times the previous threshold splits the market the same way: better-capitalised exchanges on one side, the priced-out activity moving further from regulatory view on the other.

A fidelity bond comes with it: 25% of the paid-up capital floor, roughly N500 million on top for an exchange or custodian.

Combined with the N30 million registration fee, this is not a rule smaller Nigerian founders can gradually grow into. It is a threshold that has to be met on day one, which favours foreign-backed and already-capitalised players over homegrown ones trying to formalise.

Stablecoin issuers face tiered reserve backing of 100% for naira- and commodity-backed tokens. Foreign-currency-backed tokens require 120% backing, and crypto-backed tokens require up to 200%, depending on volatility.

This closes the gap that broke USDC's peg in March 2023, when Circle's exposure to Silicon Valley Bank was invisible to anyone holding the token as a settlement instrument. Enforced properly, it puts issuer and banking-partner risk on record before a treasury takes it on.

The SEC is competing on regulatory readiness, the path Singapore and the UAE took rather than permissiveness. Kenya, Ghana, and South Africa now decide whether to match that bar or absorb the operators Nigeria prices out.

A continent-wide readiness standard and regulatory arbitrage are different outcomes. Nigeria's move has forced Kenya, Ghana, and South Africa to choose.

posts.title: A Wall Street servono mesi per saperlo. Nel Web3 basta un tweet: come l'analisi "On-Chain" rivela i movimenti dei grandi capitali.
posts.author: Andrea Mencaroni
posts.snippet:
A Wall Street servono mesi per saperlo. Nel Web3 basta un tweet: come l'analisi "On-Chain" rivela i movimenti dei grandi capitali.

A differenza della finanza tradizionale, dove le mosse dei grandi investitori rimangono coperte dal segreto per mesi prima di finire nei report trimestrali, il settore delle criptovalute offre un vantaggio informativo unico: la trasparenza radicale.
Ogni singola transazione sulla blockchain è pubblica, verificabile e tracciabile in tempo reale. Questo permette a qualsiasi investitore di fare ciò che su Wall Street sarebbe fantascienza: monitorare le mosse dei "giganti" prima che spostino il mercato.
Nel gergo crypto, questi grandi attori si chiamano Whales (Balene).
🐋 Chi sono le Balene Crypto?
Si definisce generalmente "balena" un portafoglio che detiene almeno 1.000 Bitcoin o quote massive di un determinato progetto. Principalmente si tratta di:
Fondi d'investimento e Hedge Fund istituzionali
Early adopter della prima ora
Exchange centralizzati (es. Binance, Coinbase)
Founder e tesorerie dei progetti
Quando una balena sposta i propri capitali, l'impatto sul mercato è immediato. Ma come si interpretano questi segnali?
🔍 I due segnali fondamentali dell'Analisi On-Chain
Monitorare la direzionalità dei fondi tra Wallet Privati ed Exchange è la chiave di lettura principale:
🔴 Da Wallet Privato ad Exchange → Pericolo di Vendita (Bearish) Se un grande portafoglio trasferisce 10.000 BTC verso un exchange, significa che sta preparando la liquidità per la vendita sul mercato aperto. Questo aumenta la pressione ribassista.
🟢 Da Exchange a Wallet Privato → Accumulo a Lungo Termine (Bullish) Se la balena preleva i suoi token dall'exchange per trasferirli in una custodia autonoma (Cold Wallet), significa che non intende vendere a breve. L'offerta sul mercato diminuisce, creando i presupposti per un segnale rialzista.
🛠️ Tre strumenti gratuiti per tracciare le Balene
Non servono algoritmi complessi o terminali costosi. Ecco tre risorse accessibili a tutti:
- Whale Alert (X / Twitter): Bot automatizzato che notifica in tempo reale i trasferimenti multi-milionari.
- Blockchain Explorers (es. Etherscan): Permettono di verificare saldi e storico transazioni di qualsiasi indirizzo pubblico.
- Piattaforme di Visual Intelligence (es. Arkham, Nansen): Piattaforme avanzate che tracciano ed etichettano i portafogli dei principali fondi ed entità globali.
💡 Conclusione per i professionisti della finanza e del Web3
L'analisi On-Chain non è una sfera di cristallo — le balene possono fare errori o muovere fondi per ragioni tecniche — ma rappresenta una bussola fondamentale. In un mercato efficiente e aperto, fare decisioni senza monitorare i flussi di capitale significa muoversi al buio.
💬 Voi utilizzate già l'analisi On-Chain per comprendere il sentiment di mercato, o vi affidate prevalentemente all'analisi tecnica e fondamentale tradizionale?

Bear in mind, dear reader, that everything below turns on the 'fair use' defence to copyright infringement. Only about four (4) countries out of 193 in the world have 'fair use' in their copyright laws. 

it follows that Claude, Chat GPT, Gemini, Grok and friends are almost certainly copyright infringements everywhere except, maybe, four countries. Yet they thrive. Such is our world, such have we made it.

"Anthropic Stole This From Me

Piracy is a crime as old as gold — or in the modern digital context, Napster. And intellectual property theft is pretty much baked into the A.I. development story. Most, if not all, A.I. companies built their tech on piracy — though they may call it “fair use.”

Anthropic’s story offered a twist. While many A.I. companies scraped the internet (including The New York Times, which is why OpenAI, Perplexity and Microsoft are currently being sued by the company for copyright infringement) for material, Anthropic also scanned, digitized and later destroyed physical books through a secret and expensive legal workaround.

If this was Anthropic’s legal fig leaf, it worked. The judge found that training the A.I. on physical books that Anthropic purchased was fair use, but illegally downloading and storing millions of copyrighted books, which Anthropic also did, was copyright infringement.

At $1.5 billion, ours was the largest copyright settlement in American history. Nearly half a million works were represented in our class action. After fees and lawyers (who deserve full credit for this case even existing), that works out to about $3,000 per book, which the author has to split with the publisher.

posts.title: Trust account fraud and business email compromise are the same attack. Most firms treat them as separate problems.
posts.author: CIO Tech
posts.snippet:
Trust account fraud and business email compromise are the same attack. Most firms treat them as separate problems.

The trust account redirection that the Law Society has been warning about for years is BEC. The method is email impersonation. The target is the client at the moment they expect a settlement instruction. The weapon is a spoofed domain and patience.

Most law firms have read the Law Society guidance. Fewer have made the sender domain check into a firm-wide habit, because nobody assigned ownership of the rule. It's understood in principle and unenforced in practice. Attackers rely on that gap.

The economics of the attack make it persistent. An attacker who reads a firm's inbox for two weeks, identifies one upcoming settlement worth $400,000, and sends one well-timed email has a very attractive return on effort. Even if nine out of ten attempts fail, one successful one covers the cost many times over.

The defence is not a system. It's a rule, applied by every person in the firm who touches a payment or a settlement instruction.

This week's videos cover what the spoofed settlement instruction looks like from the client's side, and how to land the phone-verification rule without a new platform or policy document.

posts.title: An IBAN might be far less sensitive than most compliance teams assume.
posts.author: Taavi Tamkivi
posts.snippet:
An IBAN might be far less sensitive than most compliance teams assume.

I keep running into the same debate: is an IBAN personal data, or something closer to a reference number? Teams default to treating it as maximally sensitive, because that feels like the safe answer.

But actually, some of the European-wide data providers already share IBAN-level information quite freely: how old an account is, roughly what volume flows in and out of it. They're clearly not treating it as a delicate piece of someone's identity, and nobody's running into regulatory trouble doing it. 

That's worth sitting with. If the market has already decided this level of detail is shareable, a lot of the caution inside individual banks is coming from assumption rather than actual legal analysis. The fix isn't to share everything. It's to stop guessing and go find out what's actually allowed.

#FinancialCrime #Sanctions

comments.text: Worth separating two questions here: is an IBAN personal data under the GDPR (almost always yes, since it's linked to an identifiable account holder), and is a given disclosure lawful under a specific legal basis or exemption in AML/CTF frameworks. The market practice you describe usually rests on the second, not on IBANs somehow falling outside personal data.

When these European data providers share account age and flow volume at IBAN level, what legal basis are they relying on - legitimate interest, a specific AML gateway, or something sector-specific that doesn't generalise to ordinary compliance teams?

We see the same pattern in crypto compliance: teams treat wallet or transaction data as radioactive by default rather than checking whether a specific disclosure is actually permitted, and the caution often has more to do with internal risk aversion than with what the law says.

💼 Myth vs Fact | Income Tax

❌ Myth: Salaried employees don't need to file an Income Tax Return (ITR) because TDS has already been deducted.

✅ Fact: TDS deduction does not automatically eliminate the need to file an ITR.

You should still file your ITR if:
✔️ Your income exceeds the prescribed filing threshold.
✔️ You have income from interest, rent, capital gains, or other sources.
✔️ You want to claim a tax refund.
✔️ You want to carry forward capital or business losses.
✔️ You need an ITR for loans, visas, or financial documentation.

Why filing an ITR matters:

- Creates a valid financial record.
- Helps claim eligible refunds.
- Ensures compliance with tax laws.
- Avoids future complications.

💡 Remember: TDS is only a method of tax collection. Filing your Income Tax Return is your responsibility if you're required to do so.

Have you ever met someone who believed that TDS deduction meant no ITR filing was required? Share your thoughts in the comments.

𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐫 8: 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐓𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲 𝐈𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐄𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡. 𝐒𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐀𝐥𝐬𝐨 𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐚𝐲 𝐘𝐞𝐬.

India now has over 6,400 climate-tech companies, and funding into this space hit close to $9.4 billion in 2024. Technology is being built.
The problem isn't the technology. It's what happens after- getting from a pitch deck to an actual government buyer, procurement team, or public rollout. That journey is where most Indian climate solutions get stuck.

𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭 1: 𝐍𝐨 𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐫𝐮𝐥𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐧

Government buying is huge in India - about 20% of GDP. But India still has no real law for green public buying.
A draft policy tried to fix this. It would have required 25-37% low-carbon steel in public projects. But someone has to check and enforce a rule like that - so the plan also included one central agency to run it. That agency got rejected in 2024. The rule never went into effect, not because the idea was bad, but because nobody was approved to run it.
So today, every climate company selling to government has to explain itself from zero, every time, because there's no shared checklist for the buyer to use.

𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭 2: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐝𝐨𝐧'𝐭 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐤 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐮𝐚𝐠𝐞

A founder can explain their tech beautifully to an investor. In front of a government buyer, the conversation often falls apart - not because the tech is bad, but because both sides are speaking differently. Founders talk about how advanced it is. Buyers need to hear cost, fit with existing rules, and what rollout actually looks like.
Take a company turning farm waste into industrial material. Saying "a brand used this to replace plastic packaging, it held up fine, and cost less" convinces a buyer faster than any deck.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐮𝐥𝐭: "𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡 𝐛𝐲 𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐬"

A company can run a dozen successful pilots and still convert zero big buyers, because each one treats it like the first time. Fewer than 3% of Indian climate startups reach Series B or further - mostly the ones depending on institutional buyers, not consumers or investors.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬:

On policy: one shared rulebook and a trained body to run it, so buyers don't need to become climate experts to approve a purchase.

On the company side: build the version of your story a government officer or procurement head can act on - cost and rollout, not just technology. And build a public brand, because buyers say yes faster to something the public already recognizes.
Building the product is only half the job. Building the case that lets someone else say yes to it is the other half.

posts.title: Pakistan does not just need a Venture Capital law. It needs a venture capital legal architecture.
posts.author: Mohtashim Ahmad Siddiqi
posts.snippet:
Pakistan does not just need a Venture Capital law. It needs a venture capital legal architecture.

SECP’s proposed standalone VC Bill is a welcome development. Particularly because it recognises a problem many of us in the ecosystem have been talking about for years: too much Pakistani venture activity ends up being structured offshore. But I don’t think regulating VC funds alone will fix that.

Last year, while working on Closing the Funding Gap for Startups in Pakistan with Invest2Innovate, Telenor and STZA, we looked at precisely this question. And the conclusion was fairly simple: capital follows certainty.

If we genuinely want Pakistan to become an attractive jurisdiction for venture capital, the reform needs to go beyond fund licensing. We need:

• clear recognition and treatment of SAFEs, convertible notes and other venture instruments;
• stronger and faster enforcement of shareholder and investor rights;
• company law that comfortably accommodates the commercial terms investors actually negotiate;
• sensible and predictable taxation for startups, funds and investors;
• seamless inward investment and repatriation of capital; and
• credible exit pathways.

Otherwise, we may create locally regulated VC funds while our best startups continue setting up holding companies in Delaware, Singapore or the UAE to actually raise capital. That would miss the bigger opportunity.

The real test of reform should not be how many VC funds Pakistan licenses. It should be how many Pakistani startups no longer need to go offshore to become investable.

SECP’s initiative can be an important starting point. But this requires SECP, SBP, FBR, BOI and the wider legal and investment ecosystem working together. 

We have an opportunity here to build the architecture properly. But solving one piece of the puzzle and calling it the ecosystem will be counterproductive.

posts.title: CFA: My failed pivot to business consulting, and tips for people without finance background.
posts.author: Ivan Chugunov
posts.snippet:
CFA: My failed pivot to business consulting, and tips for people without finance background.

By 2023, I studied and practiced law in Russia and France; M&A, bankruptcy, commercial deals. Started from scratch in Paris, then moved again to Dubai.

The pure legal path stopped being as exciting as it once was. I decided to try business consulting, and the CFA looked like a reasonable way to show recruiters I had a broader profile.
I prepped for my first attempt in May 2023 while working full-time as a lawyer. Juggling both didn’t work. As a lawyer, I had to build up the basics from zero, and I just hadn’t reserved enough time.

I passed CFA Level 1 on my second attempt, later that year, during a six-month career break. It didn’t get me a consulting job. What it did help with was my last legal role — the one right before I started Seed & Scale.

The obvious question: why would a lawyer need a CFA at all?

For me, it was about getting closer to the business side, which is where I’ve always felt most engaged. 

Working with startups rarely means dealing with law in isolation. We help shape ideas, structures and decisions earlier than people assume, and it’s hard to do that well without understanding how the business and corporate finance actually work: how money moves through a company, how incentives get built into a deal, and where the financial logic beneath a document eventually changes how you draft it.

That’s probably the most practical thing CFA gave me: more attention to the numbers behind the structure, more sensitivity to commercial logic, more comfort reading legal issues in a wider context.

My top tips for the CFA candidates:

1. Don’t start with the full curriculum. Begin with a condensed version (like Kaplan Schweser; you can even try just the Notes for some parts), do mock exams, and only go back to full readings for topics where you keep making mistakes and if you have time.

2. Start early. At least 3 months out, 6 if you’re working full-time with limited study hours.

3. During the exam, skip anything you’re stuck on, move to the next question, and circle back at the end. That was my main mistake on my first attempt.

Was a pivot attempt ever an eye-opener for any of you, for your current career path?
